sections.content: You know *tener que* + infinitive from A1 Unit 18, and *deber* from B1 Unit 4, where *deber* gives advice and *tener que* is stronger. At B2 the useful question is where the pressure comes from. *Deber* talks about a duty or a moral rule: *Debes ayudar a tus vecinos*. *Tener que* talks about a need that comes from the situation, and the speaker cannot change it: *Tengo que salir ya, porque el tren sale a las siete*. That is why *tener que* so often comes with a reason (*porque*, *si quieres*). It can also be a warm recommendation: *Tienes que probar este pastel* means "You must try this cake".
sections.title: A need, not a duty
tener que
rows: Tengo que salir ya, porque el tren sale a las siete.
I have to leave now, because the train leaves at seven.
Si quieres vivir aquí, tienes que pagar el alquiler.
If you want to live here, you have to pay the rent.
Tienes que probar este pastel; está delicioso.
You have to try this cake; it is delicious.

sections.content: *Tener que* always has a person: *tengo que*, *tienes que*, *tiene que*. When no one in particular has to do it, Spanish uses *hay que* (the next lesson). Do not use *tener que* for a rule that is the same for everybody. Later in this unit you will also see *tener que* used for a guess, as in *Tiene que ser él*.
